claims.text: Coinbase describes the hot path of its trading system as submitting and matching incoming orders against resting orders, the book.
Nasdaq executes matching orders when possible and adds non-matching limit orders to its limit order book, where they wait to be matched in price-time priority.
Coinbase's trading system is single threaded. Timers, admin requests and other logic affect trading, so they are sequenced with every other event.
It is treated as a deterministic state machine: a state plus an input always produces the same next state and output.
Running it under Raft with Aeron Cluster requires the application to be deterministic and single threaded, and makes system throughput equal to one over the application's processing time.

Trading system processing times of about 1 microsecond, a peak throughput of 300k per second, and round-trip medians under 50 microseconds with outliers under 100 microseconds in its data centre deployment.

sections.heading: How the hot path stays fast

claims.text: Coinbase uses memory-local data structures, noting that cache locality outweighs O(n), and primitive-friendly data structures that avoid boxing.
It allocates nothing on the hot path, using object pooling, and pins hot threads to fixed CPUs to prevent context switching and cache misses.
LMAX measured that a counter incremented by one unlocked thread in 300 ms took 10,000 ms with a lock on one thread and 224,000 ms with two threads sharing the lock.

recall.prompt: Why must Coinbase's trading system be single threaded and deterministic?

answer.text: Fault tolerance comes from Raft with Aeron Cluster, which requires the application to be deterministic and single threaded.

recall.prompt: With a single-threaded engine under Raft, what bounds system throughput?

answer.text: System throughput equals one over the application's processing time.

recall.prompt: Name three techniques Coinbase uses to keep the hot path fast.

answer.text: Memory-local, primitive-friendly data structures; no allocation on the hot path, with object pooling; and hot threads pinned to fixed CPUs.

recall.prompt: Why are non-trading events such as timers sequenced with orders?

answer.text: Because they affect trading logic, so they must be ordered with every other event.
